# R8 Digest — 2 Thess IV Exhortations (3:1–15) + V Letter Closing (3:16–18)
**Coverage:** Full cache slice read sequentially (slice file lines 1–485 = raw lines 6070–6554). Sections: IV. Exhortations about the Rebellious Idlers (3:1–15) — Literary Analysis, Structure, Exegesis 3:1–15, Additional Notes; V. Letter Closing (3:16–18) — Literary Analysis, Structure, Exegesis 3:16–18 (peace benediction, word of encouragement, autograph greeting + explanatory comment, grace benediction), Additional Note on 3:16. Did not stop short. No internal ebook duplication flagged. No wiki pages written.

**Source:** Jeffrey A. D. Weima, *1–2 Thessalonians* (BECNT), on 2 Thess 3:1–18.

**Priority pages:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[2-thessalonians-authorship]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]], [[1-thessalonians]]

---

## Claims

### C-R8-01 | Unit scope: third, longest treatment of rebellious idlers (ataktoi)
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** 2 Thess 3:1–15 is the letter’s second major body topic: the “rebellious idlers” (ἄτακτοι / ataktoi; cf. 1 Thess 5:14a)—members who refuse Paul’s repeated instructions on self-sufficient work, freeload on congregational charity, and use free time for meddling. Paul first addressed this on his founding visit (1 Thess 4:11b; 2 Thess 3:6, 10), again briefly in 1 Thessalonians (4:11b–12; 5:14a); the problem grew worse, so he takes it up a third time at much greater length here.
- **Quote:** "Instead of getting better, however, the problem apparently grew worse. Thus, for yet a third time and at much greater length, Paul takes up the issue here in 2 Thess. 3:1–15."
- **Locus:** slice L3; intro to IV (3:1–15)
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[1-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-02 | Structure: general (3:1–5) prepares specific discipline (3:6–15)
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** Exhortations fall into two units: vv. 1–5 “General” (pray for missionaries; reason; Lord’s strengthening/guarding; confidence; prayer) function to prepare readers to heed vv. 6–15; vv. 6–15 “Specific” frame with commands to keep away / not associate (vv. 6, 13–15), with grounds in Paul’s example (vv. 7–9) and teaching (v. 10), then application (vv. 11–12). Primary purpose is redemptive, not punitive (“brotherly” treatment, vv. 6, 15).
- **Quote:** "These disparate topics are joined together by a common function: to prepare the original readers to hear and heed the exhortations that come in the immediately following unit of verses 6–15."
- **Locus:** slice L5–L9; Structure of the Passage
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-03 | Genre: paraenesis; honor-shame force of nonassociation
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** 3:1–15 is exhortation/paraenesis (paralleling 1 Thess 4:1–5:22 after transitional prayers). Western individualistic/shameless readers easily miss the devastating impact of “keep away” / “not associate” in a communal honor-shame culture—discipline aims at shame that leads to repentance and restoration.
- **Quote:** "For the believers in Thessalonica, however, who by contrast lived in a heavily communal culture, where honor and shame were among the most powerful forces controlling social behavior, such disciplinary action would have a devastating impact (“in order that he may be put to shame”) that Paul hopes in turn will ultimately lead to their repentance and restoration."
- **Locus:** slice L7, L17, L208; Character / opening of B
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-04 | 3:1–5 and 3:6–15 are deliberately linked, not “disjointed”
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** Against commentators who split 3:1–5 from 3:6–15 and judge 3:1–5 “roughly composed”/“disjointed” (Wanamaker, Rigaux, Marshall), Weima holds the break at 3:6 is real (body-benediction in 3:5; vocative + command formula) but the first paragraph secures obedience to the second, especially via the confidence formula and the verb “command” (parangellō) linking v. 4 to vv. 6, 10, 12.
- **Quote:** "verses 1–5 are intended to secure his readers’ obedience to the specific exhortations coming in verses 6–15"
- **Locus:** slice L23–L25, L196; Extent / Exegesis link
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-05 | 3:1 to loipon + “brothers”: not “finally” as lesser topic
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** to loipon marks transition near end of a literary work but is better “as for other matters” (NIV) than “finally”; it need not introduce a lesser topic—here it opens the important idle/meddlesome problem treated at great length with strong “command” language (vv. 4, 6, 10, 12). Vocative “brothers” (sixth of seven in 2 Thess) also stresses intimacy that disposes readers to obey.
- **Quote:** "Nor does to loipon necessarily introduce a topic of lesser importance than matters previously taken up in the letter body."
- **Locus:** slice L84–L88; Exegesis 3:1
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-06 | 3:1 pray for mission: word of the Lord “run and be honored”
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** Present-tense “Pray for us” (as in 1 Thess 5:25) commands ongoing intercession; first hina-clause: “that the word of the Lord may run and be honored.” “Word of the Lord” is rare in Paul (else 1 Thess 1:8); likely subjective origin from the Lord = Jesus, not merely about him. Weima prefers athletic-race metaphor (run + victory wreath “honored”) over a firm allusion to Ps 147:4 LXX (verbal/phrasing mismatches).
- **Quote:** "the Thessalonian believers are commanded to pray for Paul that the gospel message he proclaims may not only “run” but also “be honored” (doxazētai)."
- **Locus:** slice L90–L100; Exegesis 3:1
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[1-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-07 | 3:1 “just as it also is with you”: commendation for upcoming obedience
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** Parenthesis “just as it also is with you” affirms gospel success among the Thessalonians (reality, not timing of past vs present—no verb). Functions as strong commendation that endears Paul and incentivizes obedience to the coming command (v. 6), and already shifts focus toward the readers’ situation (vv. 3–5).
- **Quote:** "The praise implied in the prayer that the gospel may succeed with all as it succeeds with the readers is designed probably as an incentive not to their prayers for him but to their obedience to the command in mind (v. 6)."
- **Locus:** slice L102–L104; Exegesis 3:1 (Frame cited approvingly)
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-08 | 3:2a deliverance from “evil and wicked people” (specific situation)
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** Second hina-clause: “that we may be rescued from evil and wicked people” (atopōn kai ponērōn anthrōpōn). Linked to mission success: proclaimers must be delivered from opponents. Against generic-threat readings (Furnish, Best), definite article + aorist “rescue” point to a particular situation (plausibly Corinth-area opposition while writing). Rhetorically creates empathy and comforts Thessalonians that God can rescue them too.
- **Quote:** "the presence of the definite article to describe those from whom he prays to be rescued—from “the evil and wicked people”…—strongly suggests that the apostle has particular people and a specific situation in mind."
- **Locus:** slice L106–L112; Exegesis 3:2a
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-09 | 3:2b “For not everyone has faith”: hinge justifying prayer and encouragement
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** “For not everyone has faith” is litotes (understatement); pistis here is human response of belief, not “the Faith” as system. Far from banal, it is a hinge: justifies mission and rescue prayers (many unbelievers need the word yet threaten preachers) and the following encouragement that the Lord must guard the Thessalonians from the evil one.
- **Quote:** "Therefore, the brief statement “For not everyone has faith,” far from being “banal and unnecessary” (Marshall 1983: 214), functions as an important hinge verse, justifying not only the previous verse but the following verse as well."
- **Locus:** slice L115–L121; Exegesis 3:2b
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-10 | 3:3 “Faithful is the Lord” = Jesus; will strengthen and guard from the evil one
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** Double wordplay (pistis → pistos; ponēros people → ponēros one) transitions from “us” to “you.” Formula “Faithful is the Lord” differs from Pauline parallels that say “God”: here kyrios is Jesus Christ (consistent with letter’s Lord-emphasis; scribes “corrected” to theos). Lord will “strengthen” (stērixei; cf. 2:17b; persecution and/or idler-obedience) and “guard” (phylaxei) from “the evil one” as personal Satan (not abstract neuter “evil”), without promising a hardship-free life.
- **Quote:** "Paul therefore is stressing to his Thessalonian readers that “the Lord” (= Jesus Christ) is “faithful.” … “who will strengthen and guard you from the evil one.”"
- **Locus:** slice L126–L138; Exegesis 3:3
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-11 | 3:4 confidence formula: “what we command you are doing and will do”
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** Confidence formula (pepoithamen en kyriō eph’ hymas) is a contemporary epistolary device that pressures recipients to live up to praise. Confidence is grounded “in the Lord,” not in the people alone. Content—“what things we are commanding, you are indeed doing and will continue to do”—looks ahead to 3:6–15 (work/discipline), not back to prayer; present tense covers repeated past + present commands. Affirms majority obedience while pressuring idlers and softening “command” language.
- **Quote:** "There can be little doubt, therefore, that the referent of the action “we are commanding” is found not by looking back to the call for the Thessalonians to remember Paul in prayer in verse 1 … but by looking ahead to the commands in verses 6–15"
- **Locus:** slice L143–L151; Exegesis 3:4
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-12 | 3:5 body-benediction: Lord direct hearts to God’s love and Christ’s endurance
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** Closing prayer of 3:1–5: “May the Lord direct your hearts to God’s love and to Christ’s endurance.” “Lord” = Jesus (as in 2:16–17). kateuthynai is imperatival optative of confident expectation; metaphorical “direct hearts” (LXX ethics). First genitive subjective: God’s love for them (cf. 2:16; Rom 5:5 etc.) steels obedience. Second genitive: Weima prefers subjective “Christ’s endurance” (esp. passion) as parallel example/ground for proper behavior in vv. 6–15, not primarily “patient waiting for Christ” or “steadfastness to Christ.”
- **Quote:** "Paul prays that the Lord Jesus will direct the hearts of the Thessalonian believers in a single-minded way both to God’s love for them and to Christ’s exemplary endurance so that they will respond with compliance to the specific injunctions he is about to give"
- **Locus:** slice L156–L176; Exegesis 3:5
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-13 | atakt- = “rebellious idlers”; cause of idleness uncertain
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** Root atakt- (vv. 6, 7, 11; 1 Thess 5:14) combines general insubordination (to leaders and Paul) with specific refusal to work—hence “rebellious idlers” (“deliberate, disobedient idleness,” Frame). Why idle? Traditional eschatological excitement vs sociological (labor disdain; patron-client freeloading). Evidence tilts somewhat to eschatological, but Weima (with Fee) judges definitive answer unavailable and largely non-decisive for meaning/application.
- **Quote:** "These two aspects are captured well in the description of such erring believers as “rebellious idlers”—those who were not merely lazy but who compounded their sin by rebelliously refusing to obey the command of both their congregational leaders and even Paul himself."
- **Locus:** slice L185–L187; intro to B (3:6–15)
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[1-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-14 | 3:6 command in the name of the Lord Jesus: keep away from ataktōs walkers
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** Opening command formula uses harsh parangellomen (not usual parakaleō) because third address to worsening idleness; addressed to whole church (“you… brothers”), not leaders only; authority “in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” makes the command ultimately Christ’s. Content: “keep away” (stellesthai… apo; rare stellō middle ≈ stand aloof) from “every brother who continues to walk… ataktōs and not according to the tradition they received from us.” Still “brother,” not “enemy” or faithless outsider (v. 2).
- **Quote:** "Now we command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you keep away from every brother who continues to walk in a rebelliously idle manner and not according to the tradition that they received from us"
- **Locus:** slice L194–L212; Exegesis 3:6
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-15 | 3:6 textual: parelabosan “they received” preferred; idlers without excuse
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** Four MS readings of the relative-clause verb; strongest, most difficult, and origin-explaining is παρελάβοσαν (“they received”). Third-person plural shows the erring members truly received the tradition and have no excuse. (Additional note also defends inclusion of ἡμῶν “our” in “our Lord Jesus Christ.”)
- **Quote:** "the third-person plural “they” indicates that the erring church members have truly been taught to live differently and thus have no excuse for their rebelliously idle behavior."
- **Locus:** slice L212, L370; Exegesis 3:6 + Additional Notes
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-16 | 3:7–9 imitate Paul: not idle; did not eat free bread; labor and toil night and day
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** First ground for v. 6: disclosure formula “you yourselves know how it is necessary to imitate us.” Antithesis: (neg.) we were not idle (atakt- = idle here); we did not eat bread from anyone as a free gift (δωρεάν; “eat bread” Semitic = daily needs); (pos.) working in labor and toil night and day so as not to burden anyone. Imitation theme forms inclusio (vv. 7, 9); model grounded in imitating Christ; educational use of exemplar.
- **Quote:** "but we were working in labor and toil night and day in order not to burden any of you"
- **Locus:** slice L217–L271; Exegesis 3:7–8
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[1-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-17 | 3:9 apostolic right waived to give a τύπος for imitation
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** Elliptical 3:9 advances (does not digress from) the example argument: Paul had the exousia (right) to support without manual labor (cf. 1 Cor 9) yet waived it “in order that we might give ourselves to you as an example so that you might imitate us.” A fortiori: if the one with the right worked, how much more should idlers without that right work. Refusal of support during founding also avoided obstacle to the gospel (1 Cor 9:12); later established churches (e.g. Philippi) could support him.
- **Quote:** "if Paul, who had a right not to engage in physical labor but instead receive support from the church, nevertheless voluntarily worked hard and long to provide for his own basic daily needs, how much more should the rebelliously idle members who do not have this right follow the example of Paul and earn their own living"
- **Locus:** slice L273–L279; Exegesis 3:9
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-18 | 3:10 teaching: “If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat”
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** Second ground (kai gar coordinating with first gar): during founding visit Paul “repeatedly commanded” (imperfect) this maxim as “tradition.” Differs from proverbial parallels by being a moral imperative and by targeting those “not willing” (ou thelei) to work—not the unemployed, ill, injured, or aged. For the unwilling: withhold food/basic needs as part of discipline (vv. 6, 14); for the genuinely needy: do not grow weary in doing good (v. 13).
- **Quote:** "If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat" … "The fundamental problem of the rebellious idlers is not their lack of employment but their deliberate refusal to work."
- **Locus:** slice L284–L292; Exegesis 3:10
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-19 | 3:11 report: some walk ataktōs—not busy but busybodies (paronomasia)
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** Application: “we hear” marks shift to current situation (oral report; not only recently discovered—idleness goes back to founding). “Some” (plural) implies more than one or two. Wordplay ergazomenous / periergazomenous: not working but meddling as busybodies (periergazomai = intrusive busybody). Inner- vs public-setting of meddling cannot be fixed with confidence. Weima attributes the pun more to Paul than to a known proverb (contra Witherington on Demosthenes).
- **Quote:** "by not being busy but by being busybodies" … "some in the Thessalonian congregation are refusing to work and using their resulting free time to meddle into the affairs of others."
- **Locus:** slice L297–L307; Exegesis 3:11
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-20 | 3:12 to the idlers: work with quietness and eat their own bread
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** Only place addressing the group more directly (“to such people,” not second-person “you”); still community-framed. Double verbs “we command and appeal” (unique): command asserts authority; appeal injects pastoral pleading/empathy (not mere maximal authority stack). “In the Lord Jesus Christ” holds authority and shared relationship. Content echoes vv. 7–10: eat their own (emphatic heautōn) bread by working with quietness (hēsychia = calm non-disturbing manner, not silence)—antidote to busybodying; cf. 1 Thess 4:11.
- **Quote:** "To such people we command and appeal in the Lord Jesus Christ that they eat their own bread by working with quietness"
- **Locus:** slice L309–L319; Exegesis 3:12
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[1-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-21 | 3:13 do not grow weary in doing good (to the genuinely needy)
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** Shift with emphatic “you… brothers”: “do not be discouraged in doing good” (mē enkakēsēte kalopoiountes). enkakeō = lose heart in desirable conduct; kalopoieō here = ongoing material charity, not vague moralism. Against readings that keep feeding the idlers: that would contradict v. 10 and undercut keep-away / nonassociate. Intended recipients are believers genuinely in need; church must not overreact by abandoning all benevolence when cutting off freeloaders.
- **Quote:** "Paul is rather warning against overinterpretation of his directions." … "Paul has in view those believers who, unlike the rebellious idlers, are genuinely in need"
- **Locus:** slice L330–L336; Exegesis 3:13
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-22 | 3:14 note the disobedient and do not associate so he may be shamed
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** First-class condition expects some will not obey “our word through the letter” (primarily the v. 12 command, not the whole epistle as independent unit). Imperative sēmeiousthe: take special notice for censure (corporate, whole congregation). Purpose: mē synanamignysthai—not associate (echoes v. 6 stellesthai; cf. 1 Cor 5:9, 11). Not full excommunication of all contact (v. 15 presupposes interaction); minimally exclude from worship/Lord’s Supper communal meals and private hosting that would feed them; further goal: put to shame (entrapē) as honor-shame restorative pressure toward return.
- **Quote:** "take special notice of that person so as to not associate with him in order that he might be put to shame"
- **Locus:** slice L338–L346; Exegesis 3:14
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-23 | 3:15 not as enemy but admonish as brother (redemptive inclusio)
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** Antithetical clarifying commands (kai, continuity not contrast with v. 14): never consider him an enemy; admonish (noutheteō = warn with blame, not mere instruct) as a brother. Love/restorative attitude; singular non-vocative “brother” at open (v. 6) and close (v. 15) is intentional inclusio marking loving discipline bounds of 3:6–15.
- **Quote:** "And do not consider him as an enemy but admonish him as a brother" … "this intended inclusio functions not only literarily to mark the boundaries of this passage (vv. 6–15) but also thematically to highlight the “brotherly” or loving way that discipline ought to be carried out in the church."
- **Locus:** slice L348–L356; Exegesis 3:15
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-24 | Letter closing (3:16–18) recapitulates body themes (Weima method)
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** 3:16–18 is the fourth major section: letter closing. Pauline closings are carefully constructed and hermeneutically significant—they reverse the thanksgiving by encapsulating main body concerns (Weima 1993; 1994a; 1995; 2010b). Structure: peace benediction (16a); word of encouragement (16b); autograph greeting + explanatory comment (17); grace benediction (18).
- **Quote:** "A detailed and comprehensive analysis of the Pauline letter closings in general reveals that they are carefully constructed units, shaped and adapted in such a way that they are related to—sometimes even summarize—the major concerns and themes addressed in the body"
- **Locus:** slice L404, L418–L424; Literary Analysis V
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]], [[paul-apostle]]

### C-R8-25 | 3:16a Lord of peace give peace at all times in every way
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** Peace benediction uniquely substitutes “the Lord” for usual “God,” adds intensive autos, and uses transitive “give… peace” with double “peace.” Emphasizes Christ (day-of-the-Lord concern 2:2; Lord throughout ch. 3) and peace needed for internal discipline tensions (cf. 1 Thess 5:13) plus broader troubles: persecution (ch. 1), eschatological anxiety (ch. 2), social trouble (ch. 3)—hence “at all times in every way.” Prefer τρόπῳ “way” over τόπῳ “place” (Additional Note).
- **Quote:** "May the Lord of peace himself give you peace at all times in every way" … "the plea for peace should be understood as broadly as this phrase and the larger context demand."
- **Locus:** slice L435–L443, L480; Exegesis 3:16a + Additional Note
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[1-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-26 | 3:16b “May the Lord be with you all” (Jewish greeting christologically adapted)
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** Unusual added encouragement (else only 1 Thess 5:24). Jewish greeting “May the Lord be with you” (Ruth 2:4 etc.) is adapted: (1) “Lord” = Christ, not Yahweh-as-God alone (attributes transferred); (2) adjective “all” includes both the fearful majority and the disciplined minority.
- **Quote:** "Paul has appropriated what strictly belonged to Yahweh in an Old Testament passage and applied it directly to Christ." … "May the Lord be with you all."
- **Locus:** slice L448–L452; Exegesis 3:16b
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-27 | 3:17 autograph greeting: secretary then Paul’s own hand
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** “The greeting is in my own hand, that of Paul.” Common practice: amanuensis writes body; sender writes closing. Phrase “in my own hand” five times in Paul implies secretary until this point (cf. Rom 16:22 Tertius). Paul often names the shift because letters are read publicly, so handwriting change is not visible to all. “Greeting” (aspasmos) is the greeting itself, not a label for the peace wish of v. 16 (against Best).
- **Quote:** "unlike everything in the letter thus far is written not by Paul’s secretary but by the apostle himself: “The greeting is in my own hand, that of Paul”"
- **Locus:** slice L457–L461; Exegesis 3:17
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]], [[2-thessalonians-authorship]]

### C-R8-28 | 3:17 “sign in every letter”: the handwriting, not the greeting formula
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** Unique explanatory comment: “which is a sign in every letter; this is the way I write.” Neuter relative ho points to the whole clause (handwritten character), not masculine “greeting.” Greeting formulas are not in every letter; “this is the way I write” = manner of closing with autograph. Implies Paul always ends with an autograph even when unstated (e.g. likely 1 Thess 5:27 singular “I cause you to swear”; Gal 6:11 already written).
- **Quote:** "The “sign,” therefore, has in view the handwritten script of Paul. … “this is the way I write” (houtōs graphō) refers to the manner in which Paul closes his letters (i.e., with an autograph) and not to the content of his closing (i.e., with a greeting)."
- **Locus:** slice L463–L465; Exegesis 3:17
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[1-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]], [[2-thessalonians-authorship]]

### C-R8-29 | 3:17 Weima: authority/presence, not mere anti-forgery authenticity
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** Majority of commentators read the “sign” as authentication against a forged letter (2:2); e.g. Danker/BDAG “mark of genuineness.” Weima argues different or at least additional purpose: (1) ancient autographs served multiple functions (legal binding, personal touch, confidentiality), not only authenticity; (2) Weima’s reading of 2:2/2:15 locates false day-of-the-Lord teaching more in a prophecy claiming Paul’s authority than in a forged letter—so primary concern here is not proving this letter genuine. Prefer: autograph intensifies personal, authoritative presence so words are harder to ignore—especially for rebellious idlers who may not obey (3:14 first-class condition). Thus 3:17 bears on authorship debates as evidence of Paul’s own hand and of his claim that such a hand-sign is his practice “in every letter,” but Weima resists reducing it to an anti-pseudepigraphy authentication device alone.
- **Quote:** "A couple of factors, however, suggest a different or at least additional purpose. … Another possibility is that the autograph makes Paul’s presence more powerfully experienced by the Thessalonian readers and thus enhances the letter’s authority. … “serves to suggest the personal, authoritative presence of the apostle in the letter.”"
- **Locus:** slice L467–L469; Exegesis 3:17 (Menken, Witherington cited)
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[2-thessalonians-authorship]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-30 | 3:18 grace with you all; chiastic inclusio with opening grace and peace
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** Grace benediction ends every Pauline letter; here unique addition of “all” (parallel to 16b) deliberately embraces the whole community—including those needing correction. Together with 3:16 peace, forms inverted/chiastic inclusio with opening “grace and peace” (1:2), framing the letter.
- **Quote:** "May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all" … "it is perhaps his own offering of the right hand of fellowship to some who otherwise need correction in order to be part of the ‘all.’"
- **Locus:** slice L474–L476; Exegesis 3:18
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-31 | Textual notes of secondary interest (3:1, 3:3, 3:8, 3:13–14)
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** Additional Notes: some MSS replace “word of the Lord” with “word of God” (3:1); some replace “Lord” with “God” in 3:3 to align formula; genitive “night and day” (3:8) preferred over accusative—periodic work within night/day, not hyperbolic continuous 24h; original ἐγκακήσητε (3:13); original infinitive συναναμίγνυσθαι (3:14) not later dual imperatives. These support lectio difficilior choices already used in exegesis above.
- **Quote:** "The genitive reading is supported by both the older MSS and Pauline practice… The accusative reading likely came about under the influence of its occurrence in the Gospels and Acts"
- **Locus:** slice L360–L378; Additional Notes on 3:1–15
- **Targets:** [[2-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R8-32 | Continuity with 1 Thessalonians on work and idlers
- **Claim (attributed Weima):** Throughout, Weima reads 2 Thess 3 as escalation of 1 Thess material: same problem (4:11b–12; 5:14a), same self-support motif (2:9), softer “appeal/admonish” in first letter → stronger “command” here; peace concern after discipline anticipated already in 1 Thess 5:12–14; prayer request “Pray for us” repeats 5:25 with content filled in. Supports treating the two letters as a coordinated pastoral sequence under Pauline authorship as Weima assumes in exegesis.
- **Quote:** "Whereas in the previous letter he settled for a brief exhortation… here the apostle feels the need to address the issue in a much longer and more direct fashion, almost certainly because the problem has grown worse instead of better."
- **Locus:** slice L3, L189, L200, L221; various (esp. intro + 3:6, 3:10)
- **Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[2-thessalonians]], [[2-thessalonians-authorship]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]
